orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It correctly located the root cause in Django’s `EnumSerializer`, implemented the appropriate name-based serialization (`EnumClass['NAME']`), and—crucially—anticipated and validated broader consequences (e.g., `re.RegexFlag` also being an enum), checking round-trips and edge cases. Transcript 2 also finds and patches the serializer, but then gets derailed by an ad-hoc test setup causing many unrelated failures, attempts brittle/incorrect test rewrites, and struggles with encoding/tooling, showing weaker debugging judgment and solution integration.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly locates the precise root cause (`EnumSerializer` using `.value`), implements the correct stable-name serialization, and then performs thoughtful validation against the reported i18n failure mode. It also anticipates and investigates knock-on effects (e.g., `re.RegexFlag` being an `Enum`), verifies round-tripping, and adds a release note, demonstrating broader system awareness. Transcript 1 makes the core code change but then thrashes on running/updating tests (path/config issues, brittle replacements, and accumulating unrelated failures), indicating weaker debugging and integration skill.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly identifies the regression’s root cause via Django’s commit history (#29260 and the follow-up #31071), applies the upstream-validated fix (`not raw` guard) in the right location, and updates/adds the appropriate regression tests and release notes. It also verifies behavior by reproducing the failure, confirming tests fail without the patch and pass with it, and checking broader suites for regressions. Transcript 2 proposes an incorrect alternative (changing insert-optimization semantics for explicitly-set PKs), which breaks an existing core test expectation and then devolves into exploratory debugging without a coherent, completed fix.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly identifies the relevant upstream fix (ticket #31071) and applies the minimal, correct change (`not raw`) that addresses the loaddata/fixture regression while preserving the insert-optimization from #29260. It also updates the associated tests and release notes, verifies failures before/after, and runs broader test suites to ensure no regressions. Transcript 1 goes down an incorrect path (trying to infer “explicit pk” via `pk_val is None`), breaks an existing optimization test, and never converges to the known correct fix within the shown work.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it performs a full debugging workflow: reliably reproduces the crash, identifies the root cause (unique constraints being introspected as indexes), implements a minimal targeted fix, and—critically—adds a regression test that fails without the patch and passes with it. It also validates the fix across relevant test suites and an end-to-end migration scenario. Transcript 2 does find and apply essentially the same fix, but it contains missteps (broken migration state attempt, a tool-call error) and lacks a proper regression test and broader verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only diagnoses and fixes the root cause (unique constraints being introspected as indexes, causing `_constraint_names(index=True)` to match both) but also adds a targeted regression test and validates it by showing it fails without the patch and passes with it. It demonstrates stronger end-to-end engineering rigor by running relevant Django test suites and an e2e makemigrations/migrate scenario, while Transcript 1 stops after a local reproduction and code tweak without integrating a proper test or broader verification. Transcript 2’s workflow is clearer, more systematic, and closer to upstream-quality contribution standards.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it makes a minimal, correct change directly in `QuerySet.in_bulk()` by consulting `opts.total_unique_constraints` for single-field unconditional `UniqueConstraint`s, preserving existing semantics and error messaging. It also validates behavior with a focused reproduction and runs the relevant Django test suites successfully (including a simulated upstream-style test) while keeping the final diff limited to the intended file. Transcript 2 is more invasive (introduces a new `Options.unique_fields` API), risks broader compatibility issues, and shows less disciplined testing and workflow (attempts to run nonexistent/incorrect test targets and encounters unrelated failures without a clean end-state).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it implements the fix in the smallest appropriate place (the `QuerySet.in_bulk()` uniqueness check) by leveraging Django’s existing `opts.total_unique_constraints`, correctly excluding conditional and multi-field constraints. It also demonstrates stronger engineering practice by adding targeted verification (including edge cases) and running substantial portions of Django’s test suite, while keeping the patch minimal and avoiding invasive API additions. Transcript 1 is more error-prone and over-invasive (adds a new `Options.unique_fields` cached_property via brittle text replacement and alters core metadata APIs), with shakier test validation and unnecessary complexity.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it quickly located the exact upstream Sphinx fix (via git history), applied a clean patch that updates option parsing, member-filtering semantics, and documentation, and validated behavior with targeted tests. It also noticed and controlled for unrelated, pre-existing test failures in the environment. Transcript 2 implemented an ad-hoc change that misses important integration details (notably merging `:private-members:` into `:members:` when `:members:` isn’t provided) and ends with incomplete/failed validation attempts, indicating weaker understanding of Sphinx autodoc’s option-processing flow.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly identifies the exact upstream implementation for the requested feature (via git history), applies the precise patch cleanly, and updates all the necessary parts: option parsing (`members_option` for `private-members`), merging behavior (`merge_members_option`), filtering logic (properly handling `None` vs `ALL` vs explicit lists), and documentation/deprecations. Transcript 1 implements a partial, ad‑hoc change that alters semantics (treating `private-members: None` as `ALL`), misses the needed merge behavior, and leads to inconsistent behavior and avoidable test issues.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it reproduces the bug with a minimal Sphinx project, pinpoints the exact parsing failure, finds the relevant upstream fix/commit, and applies the correct minimal change (`split` → `rsplit`) with an appropriate CHANGES entry. It then validates the fix with targeted and broader tests and isolates unrelated pre-existing failures. Transcript 2 eventually lands on a working but overly complex custom parser after multiple failed patch attempts that temporarily broke the file structure, indicating weaker debugging and patch discipline.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly reproduces the bug, correctly localizes the root cause to `DocFieldTransformer`’s parsing of `:param type name:` fields, and finds the exact upstream fix commit that addresses it. It applies the minimal, correct change (`split` → `rsplit`) and validates it with a targeted repro and relevant tests, aligning with established project history and intent. Transcript 1 eventually reaches a working fix but takes a more error-prone path (failed patch attempts, unnecessarily complex custom parser) and provides less clean, upstream-aligned resolution.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it delivers a complete, realistic git-over-SSH workflow matching the user’s exact `git clone user@server:/git/server` requirement by setting up `sshd`, creating a user, and testing via actual SSH. It also handles container constraints (no systemd), validates services listening on ports 22 and 8080, addresses permissions/hook edge cases, and provides a restart script. Transcript 2 only tests a local filesystem clone/push (not SSH), doesn’t set up an SSH git access path, and leaves issues like the 403 at `/` unaddressed, indicating a less thorough implementation.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it anticipates and handles real-world operational issues beyond the happy path: it installs and starts both nginx and sshd in a non-systemd environment, verifies the exact `user@server:/git/server` SSH workflow end-to-end, and adapts when `sudo` is unavailable. It also improves robustness (branch-aware hook loop, permissions/readability considerations), fixes an observed hook error, and leaves the system in a clean “pristine” state with a restart helper script. Transcript 1 works in a simplified local test but doesn’t validate the SSH-based clone/push flow the user specified and omits service/startup and permission hardening details.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger system-debugging and problem-solving: it diagnoses multiple independent blockers (missing perl LZMA module, AVX2-incompatible John binary, missing build deps, mis-specified wordlist path, and CPU cgroup throttling), then methodically fixes them and validates each step. It also uses the appropriate tooling for 7z cracking (7z2john + John) and successfully rebuilds software to match the host CPU. Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds but shows more trial-and-error (installing the wrong John version lacking 7z support, failed format listing/help attempts) and falls back to a slower custom brute-force approach.

Transcript 2 shows markedly stronger systems competence and troubleshooting: it quickly diagnoses the AVX2 mismatch, installs the correct Perl dependency via apt (instead of a lengthy CPAN build), rebuilds John with the right CPU features and missing libraries (zlib/bz2/OpenSSL), and manages tool timeouts by backgrounding and polling the build. It also notices and fixes the incorrect wordlist path, monitors cracking status effectively, and verifies extraction and file content before writing the final solution. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but with much more flailing (failed John apt version, unnecessary compilation attempt, CPAN detours, and a slower brute-force approach with extra package installs).

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger investigative skill and solution robustness: it inspects the custom libstdc++ patches to identify the precise mechanism, confirms the crash with gdb, and then iterates after discovering an initial “use_facet” warmup can be optimized away under `-O2`, ultimately choosing a warmup path that must execute library-compiled virtual facet code. It also validates the fix with targeted gdb breakpoints, repeated runs, and careful Valgrind interpretation (including verifying the “still reachable” block is baseline). Transcript 2 finds the general cause and applies a plausible warmup, but does less to ensure the trigger cannot be optimized out and provides less rigorous confirmation of the exact registration timing/allocation path.

Transcript 2 shows a deeper, more reliable diagnosis: it inspects the in-house libstdc++ patches under `/build/patches`, confirms the exact crash mechanism (facet registration allocating via `operator new` in NDEBUG, then freed after the custom heap is destroyed), and validates the trigger site with gdb. It also corrects an initial ineffective fix by recognizing optimizer/instantiation issues and then forces facet registration via a library-side virtual path (formatting a `double`) with an optimizer-proof observable effect. Transcript 1 reaches a plausible fix, but it doesn’t leverage the available patched-libstdc++ evidence and its warm-up is less robust against optimization/elision edge cases.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it derives a clean probability‑1 differential and an exact round‑key constraint, then implements an efficient intersection attack over the 65,536-key candidate set with an inlined, optimized F-function and safeguards for degenerate pairs. It also validates correctness empirically (including many random-key trials) and documents the full reasoning clearly. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working approach, but shows more trial-and-error, includes earlier incorrect hypotheses, and ends with a less optimized/less robust implementation.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it derives the full round-differential relation cleanly and correctly connects ciphertext observables (notably \(Y_3 = C_L \oplus C_R\)) to an exact constraint on \(k_5\), then implements an efficient candidate-intersection attack with an inlined fast \(f\) for speed. It also includes robustness measures (skipping degenerate pairs, collecting more constraints until unique, fallback scoring) and performs broader stress-testing, whereas Transcript 1 reaches the solution after much more trial-and-error and provides a less optimized, less defensive implementation.

Transcript 1 correctly triangulates the failing test to header control-character handling, identifies the issue as CRLF injection (CWE-93), applies a minimal, targeted fix in `_hkey`/`_hval`, writes a correctly formatted `report.jsonl`, and verifies with pytest that all tests pass. Transcript 2 initially finds the same issue but then introduces unnecessary and risky changes (e.g., adding CWE-502, attempting to replace pickle-based cookie signing), breaking tests and spiraling into incomplete/incorrect refactors. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging focus, safer patching, and better adherence to requirements.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly triangulates the real failing security issue (CRLF/control-character injection via `_hkey`/`_hval`), maps it correctly to CWE-93, implements a minimal, targeted fix that raises `ValueError` as required, and verifies with the full pytest suite. Transcript 1 is much less reliable: it misreports an unrelated CWE-502, undertakes unnecessary and breaking refactors (cookie pickle handling), and ends up with failing tests and an incomplete/derailed remediation path.

Transcript 1 shows a much cleaner, more robust end-to-end implementation: it proactively configures sshd password auth via a drop-in, sets the bare repo HEAD to `main`, uses a simple synchronous `post-receive` deploy (no missing dependencies), configures Nginx correctly with `alias` for `/dev/`, and verifies both timing and functionality—then resets to a pristine grading state. Transcript 2 reaches a working state only after multiple avoidable failures (host key issue, missing `rsync`, incorrect Nginx mapping attempts, and permission-denied errors), and never ensures a clean initial state or correct default branch configuration upfront.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it sets up the full system cleanly and correctly on the first pass: it configures sshd via a drop-in file, sets the bare repo’s HEAD to `main`, uses a simple and reliable `post-receive` hook with direct `--work-tree` checkouts, and provides a correct Nginx `alias` configuration for `/dev/`. It also validates service state, performs an end-to-end test that matches the grading procedure, measures deployment latency, and restores a clean baseline for grading—whereas Transcript 1 requires many iterative fixes (missing rsync, incorrect Nginx path handling, permission issues, and manual redeploys).

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially greater technical depth and problem-solving capability: it benchmarks multiple approaches, drills down into LAPACK driver-level differences, diagnoses subtle ABI issues (e.g., Fortran hidden string-length args, layout/copy mistakes), and ultimately builds a specialized C/NumPy extension with careful residual validation and robustness testing to achieve multi‑x speedups. Transcript 2 mostly swaps in SciPy wrappers and a 2×2 closed form, with limited optimization headroom and some inconsistent speed outcomes, and it never reaches the same level of low-level performance engineering.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially greater capability: it explores multiple algorithmic avenues, correctly identifies bottlenecks, leverages LAPACK at a lower level, and ultimately implements a compiled CPython/Numpy extension to remove Python overhead—achieving multi‑x speedups while maintaining correctness across extensive adversarial testing. Transcript 1 is competent but largely stays within high-level SciPy/Numpy calls with a small 2×2 shortcut and only modest speed gains, and it shows less depth in diagnosing performance limits. The breadth, rigor, and systems-level optimization in Transcript 2 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 shows a much deeper understanding of the evaluation model, correctly identifying that `S_max` is derived from the true aligned prompt lengths rather than the declared `shape`, and then exploiting this to minimize compilation cost by using only 2 shapes total. It implements a principled per‑S dynamic program with tuned Lagrangian weights and adds a targeted “surgical” post-pass to control p95 latency inflation, achieving stronger margins and robustness. Transcript 2 relies on a simpler heuristic (fixed 8-shape set + gen_len windowing) with tighter margins (especially bucket 2 sequential timecost) and more trial-and-error/tooling hiccups, indicating lower capability.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially deeper understanding of the cost model (notably that runtime batch S_max depends on true aligned prompt lengths, while the declared shape mainly drives compilation cost), and exploits that insight to reduce unique shapes to 2 and improve margins. It develops a more principled optimizer (DP-based partitioning plus a targeted post-pass to control p95 inflation), includes systematic sweeps/tuning, and ends with stronger, more robustly validated results. Transcript 1 reaches passing thresholds with a simpler heuristic, but with tighter margins and less model-aware optimization.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger operational competence: it inspects the Mailman/Postfix integration details (including confirmation-address behavior), writes a clean `/etc/mailman3/mailman.cfg`, configures Postfix correctly for both local mbox delivery and Mailman LMTP transport, and validates join/leave/post flows before running `/app/eval.py` successfully multiple times. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working state, but does so via repeated trial-and-error, temporarily breaking requirements (Maildir vs mbox), adding unnecessary components (installing procmail), and encountering avoidable issues (incorrect `mailman shell` usage, repeated `initialize()` errors).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly infers the required Mailman3↔Postfix LMTP integration from the provided `eval.py` expectations and implements a clean, minimal configuration that works end-to-end. It sets the correct Postfix maps (`transport_maps`, `local_recipient_maps`, `relay_domains`, `mydestination`) and Mailman config, then validates join/confirm/leave/post flows and `eval.py` successfully with little wasted effort. Transcript 1 eventually reaches a working state but only after extensive trial-and-error, multiple misconfigurations (Maildir vs mbox), permission hacks, and even installing extra packages (procmail), indicating weaker diagnostics and planning.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger end-to-end capability: it diagnoses missing dependencies (git and python), inspects bundle refs correctly, performs the fetches from HEAD into the required branch names, completes a true two-parent merge, and cleans up problematic artifacts (.DS_Store). Most importantly, it infers the mapping in a way that generalizes (searching for a consistent periodic rule and period) and validates beyond the given examples with additional randomized tests. Transcript 2’s solution is comparatively brittle (hard-codes a mod-3 anti-diagonal rule) and leaves extraneous files, making it less likely to pass hidden tests or stricter repo hygiene checks.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it executes the full workflow more robustly and systematically: it inspects bundle refs, initializes the repo cleanly, performs the merge with correct parentage, resolves conflicts while also removing junk files, and verifies the result thoroughly. Its `map` implementation infers the period/pattern from observed non-zero cells (and even checks alternative indexing functions), which is more generalizable than Transcript 1’s hard-coded mod-3 anti-diagonal approach. It also includes stronger validation (signature checks, element-wise checks, randomized generalization tests, and cleanup of `__pycache__`), indicating better engineering rigor.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it anticipates and solves the key correctness gap between Python and C: Python’s integers are arbitrary precision, while Transcript 2’s C implementation uses `long long` and will overflow past about `N=92`, causing the two execution modes to disagree for larger inputs. Transcript 1 also demonstrates stronger engineering rigor by eliminating GCC warnings via a cleaner polyglot structure and validating the C big-integer implementation against an independent checker over large N. Transcript 2 works for small N but is fundamentally less robust and less aligned with the “same file, same Fibonacci output” requirement across both runtimes.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it delivers a robust polyglot that keeps Python and C outputs consistent for large N by implementing big-integer Fibonacci on the C side, whereas Transcript 1 uses `long long` and will overflow around f(93), silently diverging from Python’s arbitrary-precision results. Transcript 2 also refines the polyglot structure to compile cleanly under strict GCC warnings and demonstrates extensive validation and edge-case awareness. This combination of correctness across inputs, engineering polish, and verification indicates higher capability.

Transcript 1 is clearly the more capable response: it builds a robust, CPU‑friendly pipeline around MobileSAM with careful prompt design (box + interior point), candidate selection using IoU against the original mask, explicit connected-component enforcement, and a principled global overlap arbitration that guarantees disjoint final masks. It also anticipates real deployment issues (cgroup CPU quotas/thread oversubscription, OpenCV API differences, empty/degenerate masks, memory scaling via cropped storage, leakage clipping, determinism) and validates against multiple stress/edge cases. Transcript 2, while functional on the demo, relies on extra installs/apt packages outside the stated assumptions, uses weaker prompting and overlap handling, and violates the “only update xmin/xmax/ymin/ymax/coords_x/coords_y” constraint by overwriting the `type` column.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger engineering and modeling judgment: it uses both box + interior point prompts, selects among SAM candidates via IoU to the original annotation, enforces contiguity, and resolves overlaps with a principled per-pixel arbitration scheme rather than a single per-mask score. It also anticipates real deployment issues (cgroup CPU quotas/thread oversubscription, OpenCV API differences, empty-CSV/header parity, and memory scaling via cropped-mask processing) and validates edge cases and scale behavior. Transcript 1 is simpler and works on the demo, but its overlap resolution is comparatively fragile (global per-mask score, fallbacks that can reintroduce overlap) and lacks the same robustness/performance considerations.

Transcript 1 demonstrates higher capability by programmatically inspecting the Turtle graph, installing tooling (rdflib), computing “currently enrolled” counts with the reference date and graduation logic, and executing the final SPARQL to verify the exact outputs. It also uses a cleaner, more semantically precise “full professor” filter (STRSTARTS with “Professor”) and explicitly validates the key edge case (Sorbonne’s students mostly graduated before 2025-08-16). Transcript 2 produces a plausible query but relies on manual reasoning, initially makes a logic mistake about country aggregation, and cannot actually run/verify the query due to missing Python in its environment.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it validates assumptions by executing the query against the actual TTL using rdflib, confirming the “currently enrolled” logic (including graduation-date filtering) and the final result set. It also implements a cleaner full-professor constraint via `STRSTARTS(?role, "Professor")`, which avoids accidentally including “Associate Professor” roles that Transcript 1’s `CONTAINS(... "Professor")` filter would match. Transcript 1 produces a plausible query but cannot run tests, briefly makes (and then fixes) an output-country scoping mistake, and leaves a more error-prone definition of “full professor.”

Transcript 1 is more capable because it methodically profiled the simulation, identified the true bottleneck (constraint solve), tested multiple targeted MJCF option changes, and validated both correctness and assumptions (e.g., sweeping seeds to confirm `ncon=0` before disabling contact). It also achieved a larger speedup (~0.51 time ratio vs ~0.56–0.58) with tighter numerical validation (max diffs reported far below `1e-5`). Transcript 2 eventually finds a working solver change, but shows more trial-and-error, schema confusion, and less rigorous validation of invariants and edge cases.

Transcript 2 is more capable: it profiles the simulation to identify the real bottlenecks (constraint solve vs. collision), tests multiple computational-only option variants, and validates robustness across many random seeds (including verifying that contacts never occur before disabling them). It achieves a larger speedup (~0.50–0.51× vs. ~0.56–0.58×) while maintaining tighter correctness guarantees (max diff ~4.7e-9) and provides clearer justification for each change. Transcript 1 eventually finds a working solver change but with more trial-and-error, less systematic validation, and a smaller performance margin.
